A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ForenAgent/FABench study, with readable main text, figures, tables and equations. However, both end with references and omit the appendices or supplementary materials they cite, limiting comparison of detailed protocols, prompts and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original FABench and SIDA-Test evaluations, training-component ablations, forensic case studies and tool-usage measurements.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations, expanded comparator and ablation results, a forensic case study and tool-usage measurements.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 revises the central action mechanism: v1 describes generating Python implementations of forensic tools, whereas v2 reserves code generation for basic image operations and invokes forensic tools directly. Structured <tool_call> actions also enter the prompts, cold-start trajectory requirements and format reward. The backbone, two-stage training and four process-reward components remain.

E1.justification: Both retain FABench and SIDA-Test with authentic, synthetic and tampered image classification. Section 3.1 changes the tampered-test generator from FLUX-1-dev to FLUX-1-Fill, but v1 already names FLUX-1-Fill in dataset construction. It is unclear whether this changes represented test data or corrects the description. Newly disclosed training-source counts do not establish expanded coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 expands from 18 to 24 baselines, adding tool-equipped GPT-4.1, Qwen2.5-VL-72B and Gemini2.5-Pro, plus AIGI-Holmes, Effort and DDA. Table 2 additionally evaluates Effort and DDA on SIDA-Test. The tool-equipped group provides a substantively new comparison; previous comparators remain.

E3.justification: New evaluations equip three MLLMs with the toolbox and test InternVL3-8B and LLaVA-7B backbone substitutions. Section 3.1 also revises the stated tampered-test generator, without establishing regeneration or rerunning. Existing training budgets, image-level metrics and FABench test counts of 700 images per class remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 3 adds separate removal of all four process rewards and two alternative-backbone evaluations, extending v1's aggregate training-stage and tool-reward ablations. The synthetic-image case changes from an airplane to a bench with a different forensic sequence. Additional robustness and efficiency studies are only referenced in unavailable supplementary materials.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports evaluation seeds, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The retained eight GRPO rollouts per prompt describe training, not repeated experimental evaluation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 add comparator and ablation outcomes and revise existing scores. ForenAgent's reported accuracy/F1 changes from 88.1/88.2 to 89.5/89.4 on FABench and 80.6/80.4 to 83.1/82.9 on SIDA-Test; FABench tampered F1 decreases from 88.0 to 86.5. Qwen2.5-VL-7B overall F1 changes from 79.7 to 79.9. Tool-use counts also change, with JPEG Ghost replacing FFT as most frequent. These are revised system results, not established controlled gains between versions.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(7) retain the same first-use definitions, global-priority reward, crop indicator and weighting, coherence condition and reward aggregation. No new formal assumptions, theorem, proof or substantive derivation appears.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion narrow autonomous tool generation or construction to tool invocation, consistent with the revised interface. The other central contributions remain: FABench, two-stage training, the four-stage reasoning loop and claims of effective, interpretable forensic reasoning.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking tool-equipped baseline improvements to forensic-tool utility, individual reward ablations to logical tool use, and backbone comparisons to model suitability. It also explicitly infers efficiency from adaptive tool counts and explains that binary detectors require modification for three-class evaluation. Earlier localization limitations remain only cross-referenced.

D1.justification: v2 discloses per-generator training counts, identifies the generic high-pass tool as Laplacian, and replaces the future code-release promise with an availability statement and repository pointer. These do not establish a changed training mixture or independently verified code availability. Conversely, v1's explicit SIDA-13B specification is omitted, with detailed baseline configurations deferred to unavailable supplementary materials.

R1.justification: Section 2 expands discussion with works including IT-Detector, ST-Trace, Chameleon, Effort, AIGI-Holmes, Loki, DeepEyesV2 and Thyme, and adds relevant model-report citations. The broad positioning around combining low-level forensic evidence with multimodal reasoning remains intact.

P1.justification: There are targeted rewrites of the abstract, related work, tool-interface descriptions and experimental discussion. Numbered tool-box, cold-start and reinforcement-learning subsections become unnumbered headings, and keywords are added. The principal section order and much of the narrative remain unchanged.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column to a single-column layout, substantially resizing and relocating figures and tables. v2 adds dataset-composition charts, replaces the synthetic case visualization, arranges tool-count plots side by side and expands Tables 1–3. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

improvement.justification: Tool-equipped comparisons and individual reward/backbone ablations strengthen the empirical support beyond v1's aggregate comparisons. Training-source counts and the code-access pointer also improve documentation. The net gain is limited by absent supplementary details, omission of the explicit SIDA model size and lack of uncertainty reporting; higher revised scores alone do not establish improved paper quality.
